P1.evidence: The only genuine application read-back in the batch, and it paid off — 'Already read through your application a little bit. Already got me a little bit excited to talk to you', and later he quoted it back verbatim: 'I saw in your application you don't want to let the old man in.' That line became the spine of the whole call. Frame was three-part — where you're at, where you want to go, bridge the gap — with the fit promise attached, but no explicit what-you-need. Agreement asked and given, and the open question ran: 'tell me, Peter, what can we potentially help you out with?'

P2.evidence: Pain was probed well — 'do you then mainly mean in the morning, or is it throughout the whole day?' and 'any pains that actually stay throughout the whole day?' — which surfaced the neck pain, the chronic low back pain and the chiropractor. Nutrition was thorough with a frequency probe on the cookies and soda. But age, weight and occupation were all volunteered and never asked, and the two most consequential omissions are the health-conditions question and sleep. Neuropathy in both feet, an $8,000 clinic he is still paying for, and the fact that he is on medications did not surface until 00:50:24 — an hour into the call, after the price, and entirely because he raised them himself. On the script that is a miss, and here it is also a safety failure.

P3.evidence: Strong. 'You're saying you're not in the best condition for yourself fit-wise. So what does that sort of mean to you?' produced the whole functional-versus-aesthetic distinction. The future-state question ran properly — 'when that is all the case for you, how would that be in six months to a year?' — and produced the real driver: 'I'm trying to figure out how can I stay as active and as fit and as young now for however many years I have left.' The reflect-back was excellent, used the application language, and was checked: 'is that correct or am I missing something there?' — which is exactly what surfaced pickleball. Weaknesses: the specific can't-do-now activity and the deeper why both arrived because the prospect volunteered them, and no who-else-does-this-impact question was asked despite a granddaughter, a wife and two sons being in play.

P4.evidence: Asked whether he had ever had a trainer ('Never'), then the right follow-up: 'why do you feel like now you want to actually get that professional help from someone who actually has all of the information?' That produced the injury fear, the self-education pattern and the information-overload problem in his own words — 'it's a lot of information, almost too much, and I feel like I could be doing stuff and maybe not maximizing what I'm doing, and just basically wasting time.' The blocker question ran too — 'what's the thing that you feel like we really would need to take care of?' — answered with core strength. P90X and the yoga-versus-saxophone trade-off were volunteered rather than elicited, and the scripted information-isn't-the-problem line never ran, although the prospect effectively delivered it himself.

P5.evidence: The rep set the frame up explicitly and then only ran half of it. He said 'what we see is with the people who get the best results, they actually can sort of see what their future looks like and also in both ways, like if they do take action, if they don't' — and then asked only the positive side. The settle question did land: 'it doesn't sound like that's something you're willing to settle for, is it?' — 'No, if I can avoid it.' But there is no what-does-this-look-like-in-two-years, no why-not, and no line in the sand. With a 68-year-old whose stated fear is losing function, the negative future was the whole leverage and it went unasked.

P6.evidence: Belief was tested and confirmed — 'do you feel like, yeah, this is going to help me to live out those goals?' — 'Yeah, exactly.' Pillar-level confirmations were also taken before the price ('do you feel like with the training and the mobility, this is what I was looking for?'). But the scripted all-in question never ran in its proper form, and the version that did run came after the price as a money isolate: 'outside of the investment aspect, you feel like, yeah, I do want to do this?' The stop condition also failed in a specific way: a second decision-maker existed the whole time and was never surfaced before the offer. Asking 'is there anyone else involved in a decision like this?' before quoting would have changed the shape of the last twenty minutes.

P11.evidence: Partial payment only: a $500 refundable deposit was taken live and confirmed ('The payment method was verified'), with the $6,000 balance deferred to a Monday decision call. The Trevor onboarding call was not booked — it was made contingent on Monday. No agreement email, nothing signed, no welcome email, no Skool link, no questionnaire. What was booked cleanly was the rep's own follow-up call, Monday 10am Eastern, with the invite chased through the inbox until confirmed.

objection_plays.detail: The best-run play in the batch. Trigger appeared twice, at 00:47:59 and 00:52:43. Ran: the money-aside personal test ('outside of the investment aspect, do you want to do this?'), the partner-reaction question ('let's say you go up to your wife and you tell her about it, what's her reaction going to be?' — 'too much money, you can look up videos and do it'), a game-plan probe ('what would sort of your game plan be to sell her on it?'), the what-if-she-says-no question, and the scripted deposit fallback, which he closed. Not run: 'is there any reason she would NOT want you stronger and less in pain', and the ownership challenge — 'is this genuinely needing her input or asking permission', 'this isn't a joint decision like buying a house'. Those two were the missing lever with a man who had just said his wife's objection would be that he could do it for free.

Money was raised early and unprompted at 00:32:31 ('now I'm on a limited budget') and again after the quote. Ran: the isolate, the monthly reframe ('it's like $1,000 a month then, basically'), and an instalment offer. Not run: the open-honest-conversation permission ask, and every single financial-picture question — no cash on hand, no monthly surplus, no credit cards, no available credit, no investments. That omission is material rather than cosmetic here, because the prospect had already disclosed that he is still paying off an $8,000 medical bill on a reduced retirement income, and nobody established whether $6,000 is affordable at all.

Two doubt triggers: injury fear at 00:21:29 ('at this age, an injury could really set me back a lot') and age-suitability at 00:27:27 ('as a 68 year old, can I benefit from your program?'). Both were answered with mechanism and social proof rather than the OE moves — no certainty reframe, no bridge, no plane, no burned-before. The social proof was also thin: an unnamed woman around 65 and 'I think that always was 75, not 100% sure'. Both objections did resolve, so the outcome was fine even though the play was not run.

Trigger at 00:57:15, 'I think I need to let it settle in, in my own head' — a think-about-it distinct from the wife. No move ran. The rep went straight to 'what do you think we should do from here?' and then to the deposit. Given that this is a second, independent hesitation on top of the spousal one, leaving it untouched means the Monday call now has two unresolved objections rather than one.

The clinical gap, at its sharpest. This prospect disclosed X-ray-documented back problems, warning tremors before spasm episodes, peripheral neuropathy in both feet, plantar fasciitis and unspecified medications. There is no scripted path for any of it, so the rep improvised in the only direction the script points — he reframed the chiropractor as a band-aid, asserted the pain would go away, and closed. A play that says 'stop and get clearance' does not exist, and this call is the argument for writing one.

notes: Discovery, goals and the spousal play were all genuinely well run — this is a competent call by the standard of the batch. Two failures matter more than the score. Health conditions were never asked, so neuropathy, medication and documented spinal findings only surfaced after the price had been quoted, and the rep undermined the prospect's own clinician on the way through. And the second decision-maker was never surfaced before the offer, which is what turned a close into a $500 holding deposit.
